meta.title: LightPath Technologies — Sam Rubin's precision optics through chalcogenide infrared lenses, BlackDiamond glass, and the defense IR imaging inflection
meta.abstract: LightPath Technologies, Inc. (NASDAQ: LPTH) is an Orlando, Florida-headquartered specialty precision optics company manufacturing molded glass aspheric lenses, infrared (IR) optics including molded chalcogenide IR lenses (proprietary BlackDiamond glass), and IR imaging assemblies. The company serves three end-market clusters: (1) defense and aerospace IR thermal imaging (uncooled and cooled IR systems for soldier-portable, vehicle-mounted, airborne, and naval surveillance applications); (2) automotive LiDAR and industrial sensing (precision aspheric optics for 905nm/1550nm LiDAR and machine-vision systems); (3) telecom/datacom and broader photonics components. Strategic narrative through 2024-2026 centers on (a) the August 2024 acquisition of G5 Infrared and the broader vertical-integration push into IR imaging assemblies, (b) defense IR demand inflection driven by Ukraine + Taiwan + Middle East geopolitical demand, (c) the BlackDiamond proprietary chalcogenide glass franchise differentiation against germanium-based IR optics, and (d) the multi-year operational restructuring under CEO Sam Rubin (appointed October 2022).

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
LightPath Technologies (NASDAQ: LPTH), headquartered in Orlando, Florida, arrived at the 2024–2026 defense infrared demand inflection carrying exactly the assets the moment required: a proprietary chalcogenide glass franchise capable of substituting for Chinese-controlled germanium, and — after the February 2025 acquisition of Hudson, New Hampshire-based G5 Infrared — a vertically integrated infrared camera capability reaching from raw glass melt to finished cooled imaging assembly. Sam Rubin, appointed President and Chief Executive Officer ~~in October 2022~~ ==effective March 9, 2020== following senior positions at ~~Coherent and its predecessor II-VI Incorporated~~ ==Thorlabs and XLight==, has spent ~~thirty months~~ ==more than six years== reshaping a legacy molded-lens business into a defence IR systems franchise. The 2024–2026 period is where that thesis has begun translating into order flow.

## ~~Three Product Families~~ ==Four Product Groups==

LightPath ~~operates across three product segments~~ ==reports as a single operating segment organised into four product groups==. The legacy business — visible-wavelength precision molded glass aspheric lenses for telecom, datacom, machine vision, and medical OEMs — generated $11.7 million in fiscal year 2025 (year ended June 30, 2025), up 4 percent year on year. A second ~~family~~ ==group== covers infrared optics: molded lenses using proprietary BlackDiamond™ chalcogenide glass (grades BD1, BD2, BD6, and BDNL) alongside diamond-turned germanium and silicon elements; IR components produced $14.3 million in FY2025, up 2 percent. The third and fastest-growing ~~family~~ ==group== — engineered IR imaging assemblies — is the strategic spine of Rubin's thesis: assemblies and modules reached $8.0 million in FY2025, [up 79 percent](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lightpath-technologies-reports-fiscal-2025-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-financial-results-302567574.html), absorbing G5 Infrared's initial contribution~~, while engineering services added~~ ==. The fourth group, engineering services, added== $3.2 million, up 63 percent.

## Heritage: GRADIUM to Latvia to New Hampshire

LightPath traces its origins to 1985, when Dr. Richard Caputo and colleagues founded the company around GRADIUM, a gradient-index glass technology developed at the University of Rochester. The 2016 acquisition of ISP Optics in Riga, Latvia introduced diamond-turning capacity and chalcogenide IR expertise, seeding what became the BlackDiamond programme. The February 2025 [G5 Infrared acquisition](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/lightpath-technologies-announces-strategic-acquisition-130000599.html) — $27.0 million in consideration ($20.25 million cash plus $6.75 million in common shares, with performance-based earnouts) — was the third and most consequential step. G5 brought cooled and uncooled infrared camera systems for naval long-range surveillance, border security, and counter-UAS programmes, with preliminary calendar-year 2024 revenue exceeding $15 million. "The acquisition of G5 Infrared," Rubin said at announcement, "is a transformative step in our strategy to become a leading vertically integrated provider of infrared imaging solutions."

## Revenue Inflection

FY2025 consolidated revenue reached $37.2 million, up 17.4 percent from $31.7 million, against a net loss of $(14.9) million; gross margin was 27.2 percent. The pace has since sharply accelerated. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026 (ended March 31, 2026), LightPath reported revenue of $19.1 million, [up 109 percent year on year](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lightpath-technologies-reports-fiscal-2026-third-quarter-financial-results-302764869.html), with gross margin expanding to 36 percent and adjusted EBITDA turning positive at $1.1 million — ~~a company first~~ ==the third consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA==. The order backlog at March 31, 2026 stood at a record $110.6 million, up 196 percent from $37.4 million at the FY2025 close, anchored by an $18.2 million IR camera purchase order scheduled for calendar-year 2026 delivery, a $22.1 million follow-on for CY2027, a $2.2 million engineering development contract from L3Harris for the U.S. Navy's SPEIR programme, and $9.7 million in cooled camera orders for counter-UAS applications.

## BlackDiamond and the Germanium Substitution Thesis

China dominates global germanium production and applied export licensing restrictions beginning in mid-2023; germanium prices rose roughly 65 percent from January 2023 to October 2024. The U.S. Defense Logistics Agency's Strategic Materials office responded with a two-phase qualification programme: [Phase 1, $250,000 awarded July 2023](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lightpath-technologies-awarded-phase-2-funding-in-us-defense-department-partnership-to-qualify-additional-germanium-substitutes-302262203.html); Phase 2, approximately $500,000 awarded October 2024, targeting six additional BlackDiamond formulations to Material Readiness Level 9 for defence programme insertion. The legislative framework tightened further when the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act [directed the Department of Defense](https://www.lightpath.com/insights/what-does-fy26-ndaa-say-about-germanium-lenses-and-alternatives) to eliminate reliance on foreign optical glass by January 1, 2030. Rubin stated on the Q4 FY2025 earnings call: "Supply chain risk and Chinese critical mineral export restrictions are accelerating customer demand for Germanium alternatives, pushing them to our in-house BlackDiamond™ solution." As of Q3 FY2026, the BlackDiamond portfolio spanned approximately 20 proprietary infrared glass compositions, licensed exclusively from the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory and manufactured across two U.S. facilities following LightPath's January 2026 acquisition of chalcogenide glass specialist Amorphous Materials Inc. In August 2025 the company [announced the first germanium-free G5 camera variants](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lightpath-technologies-announces-first-germanium-free-g5-camera-variants-utilizing-proprietary-blackdiamond-glass-302520923.html) — two cooled infrared models rebuilt around BlackDiamond glass — with Rubin committing in March 2026 to "complete the redesign of G5's cooled infrared camera family onto BlackDiamond™ by the end of summer 2026."

## What This Dossier Examines

The chapters that follow interrogate the assumptions embedded in this snapshot. The $110.6 million backlog is the centrepiece: are these programme-of-record positions or early-adoption orders that could be revised? How concentrated is defence revenue across the handful of prime-contractor and system-integrator relationships visible in public disclosures — and what does that concentration mean for revenue visibility? What is the strategic outcome for the Zhenjiang, China manufacturing subsidiary given the NDAA domestic-sourcing trajectory and the broader U.S.-China critical-materials contest? And where does LightPath's cost position settle against Edmund Optics, Jenoptik, and the broader optics operations of Coherent as the chalcogenide IR lens market scales from laboratory qualification to high-volume defence production?

chapters.title: From 1985 founding through ISP Optics to G5 Infrared and the defense IR inflection
chapters.body:
## The GRADIUM Era: A Florida Optics Start-Up Built on Gradient Glass

LightPath Technologies traces its origin to 1985, when Dr. Richard Caputo and co-founders established the company in Orlando, Florida around a single proprietary technology: GRADIUM, a gradient-index glass capable of bending light through a continuously varying refractive index across the lens blank rather than relying solely on surface curvature. The concept was academically elegant—a single GRADIUM element could replace multi-element lens assemblies by doing aberration correction inside the glass itself—and the founders believed it could anchor a new class of precision optical components for telecom infrastructure, scientific instruments, and industrial applications then expanding rapidly across the United States.

Through the late 1980s and 1990s the company pursued commercialization of GRADIUM under a series of development-stage funding rounds, filing with the SEC as its capital base grew and licensing discussions with optical OEMs proceeded. The technology attracted academic and industry interest, but the commercial trajectory proved slower than the founding thesis had projected. GRADIUM required tight process control over the ion-exchange glass fabrication and found a narrower addressable market than the founders anticipated, particularly as competing lens design approaches advanced in parallel.

The telecom boom of the late 1990s provided a partial reprieve. LightPath pivoted its precision lens manufacturing capabilities toward fiber-optic collimators and related telecom components—demand driven by the explosion in wavelength-division multiplexed networks across North America and Europe. Revenue expanded and the company scaled its Orlando manufacturing operations accordingly, listing on NASDAQ under the ticker LPTH and building out a customer base of fiber-optic component and module suppliers. The bust that followed the 2001 telecom collapse was severe. LightPath, like virtually every precision optics supplier with heavy telecom exposure, suffered a sharp demand contraction and was forced through a painful restructuring of its cost base.

## Precision Aspheric Molded Lenses: The Middle Decades

Out of the telecom wreckage, LightPath rebuilt around a more durable manufacturing capability: precision aspheric glass lens molding at volume. The process—pressing heated optical glass preforms in tungsten-carbide molds under precisely controlled temperature and pressure profiles—allowed LightPath to produce near-net-shape aspheric lenses without the grinding and polishing steps that dominate conventional lens fabrication. Unit costs fell materially relative to conventional manufacture, and the resulting lenses, holding tight surface-figure and centration tolerances, found application in laser beam shaping, machine-vision optics, medical endoscopes, and the emerging LiDAR sensing ecosystem.

Through the 2000s and into the 2010s, LightPath operated from its Orlando, Florida facility supplemented by manufacturing operations established in Zhenjiang and Shanghai, China—the latter reflecting the broader industry migration toward lower-cost Asian production for volume lens supply. Revenue settled into a range of roughly $30 million to $40 million annually, with the business generating thin margins and occasional operating losses as the company balanced the capital intensity of mold tooling investment against customer pricing pressure on commodity lens programs. The Chinese operations provided cost competitiveness but also introduced the geopolitical and supply-chain exposure that would later complicate strategic planning under the Rubin administration.

## ISP Optics and the BlackDiamond Franchise: The 2016 Inflection

The most consequential strategic move of LightPath's first three decades came in 2016, when the company completed the acquisition of ISP Optics, operating from Riga, Latvia, and incorporating the acquired entity into its operations as LightPath Optical Instrumentation. The transaction brought LightPath into infrared optics—a product category structurally distinct from its visible-wavelength molded-glass business and serving a radically different end-market structure dominated by defense and security imaging.

ISP Optics brought two capabilities that would define LightPath's subsequent strategy. The first was a diamond-turning operation producing precision germanium and silicon IR optical elements—the hard-and-brittle materials used in thermal imaging lenses across military, law enforcement, and commercial security applications. The second was the BlackDiamond chalcogenide glass franchise: a family of proprietary chalcogenide glass compositions, designated BD1, BD2, BD6, and BDNL, formulated to transmit in the mid-wave and long-wave infrared bands while remaining moldable using the same precision-press technology LightPath had refined for visible glass over the prior two decades.

BlackDiamond's commercial significance was rooted in a structural vulnerability in conventional IR optics supply chains. Germanium—the dominant substrate for thermal imaging lenses—is produced overwhelmingly in China, which controls an estimated 60 percent or more of global germanium output and has deployed export licensing requirements on germanium as a strategic trade instrument. When Beijing tightened germanium export controls through 2023 and 2024, the resulting supply uncertainty accelerated customer interest in chalcogenide glass alternatives that LightPath could mold at its Orlando and Latvia facilities without dependence on Chinese feedstock. The BlackDiamond substitution thesis moved from strategic positioning to active sales argument across the company's defense and security customer base.

The ISP Optics acquisition also expanded LightPath's geographic footprint in a technically useful direction: Latvia's proximity to European defense procurement channels and NATO supply chains offered access to a customer base that the Orlando headquarters could not have cultivated efficiently on its own.

## Sam Rubin and the Engineered-Solutions Pivot: ~~October 2022~~ ==March 2020==

In ~~October 2022~~ ==March 2020== LightPath Technologies appointed Sam Rubin as President and Chief Executive Officer, effective ==March 9,== replacing the prior leadership team that had managed the company through the ISP Optics integration. Rubin arrived from ~~Coherent—the photonics and compound-semiconductor conglomerate that had absorbed II-VI Incorporated in 2022—where he had served as General Manager of the Components Solutions division, overseeing a business unit with direct relevance to~~ ==XLight Photonics, following an earlier executive tenure at Thorlabs, both of which gave him direct operating experience in== the precision optical components market LightPath served.

The strategic logic of Rubin's appointment was legible from his background. LightPath's NASDAQ listing, small-cap market capitalization, and history of thin margins reflected a company that had not fully extracted value from its technology assets—specifically the BlackDiamond franchise and the IR optics capability acquired via ISP Optics. Rubin's mandate was to shift the revenue mix away from commodity visible-wavelength lens supply toward higher-margin engineered solutions: multi-element IR assemblies, custom imaging modules, and subsystems that bundled LightPath's optical fabrication capabilities into deliverables commanding premium pricing and longer-cycle customer relationships.

The pivot entailed uncomfortable decisions about the China operations. LightPath's Zhenjiang and Shanghai facilities, which had served the volume molded-lens business for the better part of two decades, carried operating costs, management attention, and geopolitical risk that were increasingly difficult to justify against a strategic direction centered on defense-cleared IR imaging in the United States and Europe. Under Rubin, the company entered a multi-year review of those operations, weighing restructuring, wind-down, and divestiture scenarios against the remaining telecom and industrial lens volume they supported. ==Effective February 28, 2023, the Shanghai and Zhenjiang legal entities were consolidated into LPOIZ, concentrating Chinese manufacturing at the Zhenjiang facility.==

## G5 Infrared and the Defense IR Inflection: ~~August 2024~~ ==February 2025==

The Rubin administration's most significant strategic act was executed in ~~August 2024~~ ==February 2025== with the acquisition of G5 Infrared, based in New Hampshire, for terms that included a combination of cash, debt, and equity consideration. G5 Infrared was an established designer and assembler of uncooled and cooled infrared imaging modules—complete electro-optical subsystems integrating detector arrays, read-out integrated circuits, and optical assemblies into deliverable units for defense systems integrators.

The transaction represented a fundamental expansion of LightPath's value-chain position. Prior to G5 Infrared, LightPath sold optical elements and sub-assemblies to customers who performed the higher-value integration work themselves; after the acquisition, LightPath could offer complete imaging modules to defense primes including Lockheed Martin, RTX's Raytheon division, L3Harris, Northrop Grumman, Teledyne FLIR, Elbit Systems, and Leonardo DRS. The addressable revenue per defense platform program expanded materially as a result.

The timing of the G5 Infrared acquisition intersected with the sharpest multi-year upturn in defense IR imaging demand in a generation. The Russia-Ukraine war, which ~~entered its third year in 2024~~ ==entered its fourth year in 2025==, consumed soldier-portable thermal weapon sights, vehicle-mounted IR surveillance systems, and drone-optical payloads at a rate that stretched lead times across the Western IR supply chain. Simultaneously, Taiwan Strait tensions sustained elevated US and allied procurement of ISR and targeting optics, while Middle East operations generated additional near-term demand. Defense IR—long a steady if undramatic market—was suddenly a growth sector, and LightPath, through the combination of its BlackDiamond moldable IR glass, its diamond-turned germanium and silicon capability from ISP Optics Latvia, and the G5 Infrared imaging-assembly franchise, had assembled a vertically integrated IR optics-to-modules offering precisely as demand surged.

By the time of the frozen snapshot in May 2026, the company's narrative arc had traversed four decades: from a Florida start-up commercializing gradient-index glass in the late Cold War, through the telecom-boom-and-bust cycle of volume aspheric molded lenses, through the Latvia acquisition that planted the BlackDiamond IR franchise, and finally through a CEO transition and a New Hampshire acquisition that positioned LightPath as a defense-facing IR imaging pure-play at the moment when that market's structural tailwinds were strongest in a quarter-century.

chapters.title: Visible aspherics, BlackDiamond chalcogenide IR, germanium/silicon IR, IR imaging assemblies
chapters.body:
LightPath Technologies' product portfolio spans the full optical spectrum from near-visible wavelengths through the long-wave infrared, organized across ~~three commercial families~~ ==four product groups== assembled over four decades through organic development and two transformative acquisitions. The visible-wavelength molded glass aspheric business that defined the company's first generation of growth now serves as a cash-generative foundation, while the BlackDiamond chalcogenide infrared platform and the newly vertically-integrated G5 Infrared imaging-assembly capability carry the strategic weight of a defense-oriented pivot begun in earnest when Sam Rubin assumed the chief executive role ~~in October 2022~~ ==effective March 9, 2020==.

## Visible-Wavelength Precision Molded Aspherics

The original LightPath franchise was precision molded glass aspheric lenses—a manufacturing competence rooted in the company's 1985 founding and an outgrowth of early work on GRADIUM gradient-index glass technology pioneered by co-founder Dr. Richard Caputo. Precision molding presses polished glass billets against diamond-machined molds under controlled thermal and pressure cycles, producing aspheric surfaces at tolerances that would be prohibitively expensive to grind and polish conventionally. The process suits high-volume optical applications: fiber-optic collimators, laser beam-shaping elements, machine-vision field lenses, and medical-device illumination paths.

The end-market mix for visible aspherics reflects the diffuse industrial breadth of photonics. Telecom and datacom historically absorbed a meaningful fraction of LightPath's visible-lens output—pigtailed collimators for amplifier stages, isolators, and WDM multiplexers all depend on small-diameter aspherics with sub-micron form accuracy. Industrial sensing and machine-vision OEMs draw on LightPath's catalog and custom-engineered designs for inspection systems and structured-light depth cameras. Medical-device applications—endoscopic illumination, ophthalmic imaging—add a vertical where dimensional repeatability and certifiable glass compositions matter.

Automotive LiDAR emerged as the more recent demand vector. Solid-state and MEMS-based LiDAR sensors deployed by Luminar, Aeva, and Innoviz require precision aspherics in their transmit-and-receive paths to collimate 905-nanometre or 1550-nanometre pulses and focus return signals onto detector arrays. LightPath's ability to mold lenses in volume at optical-grade tolerances positioned it as a credible Tier-2 supplier into an ecosystem spending the early 2020s driving down sensor bill-of-materials costs. The production ramp remained contingent on OEM model launches and platform consolidation through fiscal 2024.

The strategic tension in visible aspherics is volume versus margin. Commodity molded lenses in standard-catalog diameters carry gross margins insufficient to fund the R&D and capital deployment management regards as necessary for the IR transition. Rubin's stated objective has been to reweight revenue away from catalog visible lenses and toward higher-margin engineered solutions and IR imaging assemblies, treating the visible-aspheric book as a stable but slow-growth base rather than a driver.

## The BlackDiamond Chalcogenide Platform

LightPath's most differentiated intellectual property sits in its BlackDiamond family of proprietary chalcogenide glass compositions—designated BD1, BD2, BD6, and BDNL—each engineered for distinct combinations of infrared transmission, refractive index, dispersion, and thermal stability. Chalcogenide glasses substitute sulfur, selenium, or tellurium for the oxygen anions of conventional oxide glasses, producing amorphous materials that transmit across the mid-wave infrared (MWIR, 3–5 micrometres) and long-wave infrared (LWIR, 8–12 micrometres) bands where germanium and silicon have historically dominated precision optics.

The strategic significance of BlackDiamond is partly compositional and partly process-based. Unlike germanium, which must be shaped by single-point diamond turning—a serial, labor-intensive process that constrains throughput—chalcogenide glasses can be press-molded using the same thermal-cycle tooling LightPath applies to its visible-wavelength aspherics. At sufficient volume, a molded chalcogenide lens is meaningfully cheaper than a diamond-turned germanium equivalent of comparable aperture and complexity. The unit-cost argument is strongest for uncooled thermal cameras where germanium's higher material cost and per-piece machining time represent a significant fraction of bill-of-materials.

The germanium substitution thesis acquired geopolitical urgency beginning in 2023. China accounts for roughly 80 percent of global refined germanium supply; Beijing applied export licensing requirements to germanium shipments in mid-2023, tightening further through 2024. Defense and commercial customers reliant on germanium-based IR optics faced both supply uncertainty and price pressure, accelerating interest in alternatives. BlackDiamond positions LightPath as a non-China source of scalable IR optics whose production is decoupled from Chinese export policy—a competitive argument the salesforce could deploy with defense procurement offices already sensitised to supply-chain provenance.

The BD1 formulation anchors the family as a germanium-arsenic-selenide system transmissive across the full 3–12 micrometre window. BD6 offers an elevated refractive index relevant for compact, fast optical designs where thick, heavy germanium elements would otherwise be required; it has featured in technical disclosures as the preferred composition for high-performance defense applications where size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints are primary design drivers. The BDNL designation targets applications requiring specific dispersion-management properties. LightPath has been deliberate about not publishing precise compositional recipes, treating the glass formulations as proprietary trade secrets rather than published patents—a posture that limits replication risk from better-resourced competitors.

## Germanium and Silicon: The Legacy IR Foundation

Before BlackDiamond achieved commercial scale, and alongside it today, LightPath manufactured IR optics by single-point diamond turning germanium and silicon blanks into precision spherical and aspheric forms. The Latvia operations acquired through the 2016 ISP Optics purchase brought meaningful diamond-turning capacity: Riga's machining infrastructure complements Orlando's molding lines and allows LightPath to serve customers whose aperture requirements, surface-figure tolerances, or qualification histories are tied to germanium or silicon substrates rather than chalcogenide glass.

Germanium remains the workhorse material for cooled MWIR detector systems where narrow detector acceptance cones demand highest surface quality and the cost of the overall sensor package makes lens material cost a secondary variable. Silicon, transmissive primarily in the MWIR, finds application in filter substrates and window elements. LightPath's diamond-turned germanium and silicon lines thus serve the higher-performance end of the defense IR market—cooled HgCdTe and InSb detector systems aboard fixed-wing platforms, rotary-wing aircraft, and naval vessels—while BlackDiamond competes more directly in the uncooled microbolometer market where SWaP and unit-cost optimisation are paramount.

## G5 Infrared and the Assembly Tier

The ~~August 2024~~ ==February 2025== acquisition of G5 Infrared—a New Hampshire-based manufacturer of uncooled and cooled IR imaging assemblies—was the most consequential single corporate act of Rubin's tenure. Prior to G5, LightPath was a components supplier: it manufactured lenses and lens sets that systems integrators and defense primes assembled into camera modules and sensor payloads. The G5 transaction moved LightPath one tier up the value chain, delivering complete imaging assemblies—lens barrel, detector, readout circuit, housing, and interface electronics—to customers who previously bought LightPath lenses and assembled the camera themselves.

G5 Infrared's catalog addressed both uncooled (microbolometer-based, ambient-temperature) and cooled (InSb or HgCdTe, cryogenically cooled) imaging configurations. The uncooled segment is volume-driven: soldier-portable thermal sights, vehicle-mounted observation systems, and UAV payloads depend on small-format, power-efficient cameras. The cooled segment serves higher-unit-value applications—targeting pods, surveillance turrets, and missile seeker assemblies—where sensitivity requirements exceed what uncooled detectors can achieve.

The integration thesis is straightforward: G5 Infrared assemblies become the primary internal customer for LightPath's Orlando- and Riga-manufactured BlackDiamond and germanium lenses, tightening vertical integration and expanding average selling price per shipped unit from a lens element priced in the low hundreds of dollars to a completed assembly at multiples more. Defense customers purchasing IR imaging assemblies from a single vertically-integrated vendor rather than managing a multi-supplier build-to-print programme reduce their procurement overhead—a selling point in an environment where contractors have been under pressure to simplify supply chains for system-level IR components.

## Engineered Solutions and Custom Integration

Alongside the ~~three~~ ==other== product families, LightPath's engineered-solutions segment captures custom design work: fiber collimators built to customer-specified beam-divergence parameters, multi-element assemblies combining visible and IR optics for dual-band sensors, and OEM-specific optical sub-systems. This segment carries the highest gross margins and has been the focus of Rubin's commercial repositioning. The revenue contribution remained smaller than the visible-aspheric and IR-optics lines in absolute terms through fiscal 2024, but management has consistently flagged it as the intended destination for incremental engineering bandwidth and sales-team attention.

## Manufacturing Footprint

The four-site production network reflects LightPath's acquisition history as much as its operational design. Orlando serves as headquarters and the primary facility for visible-wavelength precision molding and BlackDiamond chalcogenide lens production. Riga, Latvia—inherited from the 2016 ISP Optics acquisition and operating as LightPath Optical Instrumentation—provides diamond-turning capacity, optical assembly, and test capability that complements Orlando's molding strength, while offering a European manufacturing address for customers sensitive to supply-chain geography.

New Hampshire, added with G5 Infrared in ~~August 2024~~ ==February 2025==, houses the imaging-assembly operations that convert LightPath's optical components into camera-level subsystems. The China operations—~~manufacturing sites in Zhenjiang and Shanghai~~ ==a Zhenjiang manufacturing site, with the Shanghai and Zhenjiang legal entities consolidated into LPOIZ effective February 28, 2023==—have been under active strategic review since at least fiscal 2023. The geopolitical environment, combined with US government customer concerns about components manufactured in China appearing in defense-linked optical systems, created pressure to either repatriate or wind down the China footprint. Management characterised the review as ongoing through the period, with outcomes ranging from a continuing reduced-role operation serving non-defence commercial customers to full consolidation into the Orlando and Riga sites. The resolution of the China question represents one of the more consequential operational decisions facing the company through fiscal 2026.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, IR mix shift, G5 contribution, gross margin progression
chapters.body:
## Revenue Plateau, Then Inflection: Three Fiscal Years of Compression

Between fiscal year 2022 and fiscal year 2024, LightPath Technologies ran through a methodical revenue contraction that masked a more important structural story beneath the top line. Reported revenue fell from $35.6 million in fiscal 2022 to $32.9 million in fiscal 2023 and further to $31.7 million in fiscal 2024 — a cumulative decline of roughly 11 per cent across three years. The compression was not accidental; it was, in the characterisation of management, a deliberate consequence of walking away from low-margin visible-wavelength commodity lens volume while the higher-margin infrared and engineered-solutions pipeline had not yet grown large enough to fill the gap.

The visible-components ~~segment~~ ==product group==, once the revenue foundation of LightPath's legacy molded-lens franchise, contracted sharply: it fell 16 per cent year-on-year in fiscal 2024 alone, shrinking to $11.2 million — 35 per cent of full-year revenue — as telecom-adjacent volume was deliberately shed. Infrared components held steadier at $14.1 million (44 per cent of fiscal 2024 revenue) but also declined modestly, falling 2 per cent as pricing normalised and demand from LightPath's China operations softened amid a broader deterioration in the domestic industrial economy. Assemblies and modules — the emerging higher-value ~~segment~~ ==product group== representing custom thermal and optical subassemblies — contributed $4.5 million (14 per cent), while engineering services surged 363 per cent year-on-year to $2.0 million, the clearest numerical signature of the customer-intimate "LightPath 2.0" model articulated by chief executive Sam Rubin. Together, assemblies and engineering services reached 28 per cent of fourth-quarter fiscal 2024 revenue — a directional proof-point for the mix-shift thesis before G5 Infrared arrived.

## Gross Margin: A Painful Compression Before Recovery

The revenue slide was accompanied by gross margin deterioration that complicated the investment narrative. Gross margin ran at 33.2 per cent in fiscal 2022 and a marginally firmer 33.6 per cent in fiscal 2023. In fiscal 2024 it collapsed to 27.2 per cent — a 6.4 percentage-point step-down that eliminated roughly $1.5 million of gross profit on an already-shrinking revenue base. The third quarter of fiscal 2024 was the worst single quarter, recording only 21 per cent gross margin, driven by the combination of lower visible-component volumes (which carry fixed absorption costs), a structural shift toward infrared components that in commodity form carry thinner margins than polished-glass visible optics, and a net inventory write-down executed as part of cost-reduction actions across materials, labour, and outside services.

The same 27.2 per cent full-year gross margin held through fiscal 2025, though the internal composition was changing. A one-time $500,000 inventory reserve charge against the visible-components book in the June 2025 quarter compressed that quarter's reported gross margin to 22 per cent; stripping the charge, adjusted gross margin ran at approximately 29.7 per cent. CFO Al Miranda, speaking on the Q4 fiscal 2025 earnings call, described the underlying run-rate as "pretty close to 30," and the subsequent quarters confirmed a genuine recovery. Gross margin rebounded to 29.8 per cent in Q1 fiscal 2026, then jumped to 36.8 per cent in Q2 and sustained at 36.3 per cent in Q3 — surpassing the near-term 35 per cent guidance the CFO had set "within a quarter or two" and approaching the 40 per cent target he had indicated as achievable as the product mix shifted toward finished infrared camera systems.

*Sources: [SEC EDGAR LPTH filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000889971&type=10-K); [StockTitan LPTH Financials](https://www.stocktitan.net/financials/LPTH/); [PR Newswire FY2024 results](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lightpath-technologies-reports-fiscal-2024-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-financial-results-302253524.html)*

## Acquiring the Missing Link: G5 Infrared

The pivotal structural step was the acquisition of G5 Infrared, LLC, a New Hampshire-based manufacturer of uncooled and cooled IR camera assemblies serving US defence primes. The path to closing was longer than its headline implies. On 6 August 2024, LightPath entered into a $3.0 million bridge promissory note with Lytton-Kambara Foundation, carrying a 12.5 per cent interest rate and a 7 per cent original issue discount — signalling that commercial negotiations were already well advanced and that LightPath needed a short-duration liquidity bridge ahead of a more comprehensive capital raise. The formal announcement came on 13 February 2025; the acquisition closed on 18 February.

The deal structure reflected the asymmetry between a small-cap acquirer and a target with meaningful defence customer concentration. Initial consideration totalled $27 million: $20.25 million in cash and $6.75 million in LightPath common stock (1,972,501 shares). A performance-based earnout of up to $23 million, payable in fiscal years 2026 and 2027, took total potential consideration to approximately $50.2 million. The first tranche requires G5 to achieve $21 million of revenue at a 20 per cent EBITDA margin; by the time of the Q4 fiscal 2025 earnings call, CFO Miranda stated that the then-current backlog "indicates they'll hit that first mark." [LightPath 8-K, February 2025](https://www.marketscreener.com/quote/stock/LIGHTPATH-TECHNOLOGIES-IN-9910/news/LightPath-Technologies-Announces-Closing-of-Acquisition-of-G5-Infrared-LLC-49105660/)

Financing the cash component required LightPath to raise capital alongside converting the bridge. The company placed $25.5 million of 6.5 per cent fixed-price convertible preferred equity and warrants, and $5.2 million in senior secured promissory notes. CEO Rubin framed the transaction with explicit revenue ambition:

> "This accretive acquisition immediately strengthens our financial profile, creating a combined company that we believe will achieve revenue of at least $55 million in the twelve months following the acquisition."

G5 had generated at least $15 million in preliminary, unaudited revenue in calendar year 2024 before closing — establishing a base run-rate that, combined with LightPath's $31 million annual core, supported the $55 million combined-company guidance. [Yahoo Finance / LightPath press release](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/lightpath-technologies-announces-strategic-acquisition-130000599.html)

## FY2025: A Partial-Year Contribution and the First Inflection

Because the acquisition closed in mid-February 2025, G5's contribution to fiscal year 2025 (July 2024 through June 2025) encompassed only the final five months. The nine months ended 31 March 2025 showed aggregate revenue of $25.0 million — roughly in line with the pre-G5 run-rate. The June quarter changed the income-statement complexion materially: Q4 fiscal 2025 revenue reached $12.2 million, a 41.4 per cent year-on-year surge from the $8.6 million recorded in Q4 fiscal 2024, with G5 contributing $4.2 million of that total. Full-year fiscal 2025 revenue landed at $37.2 million — the first annual revenue growth in four years, and a 17.3 per cent increase on fiscal 2024.

The product-mix shift at fiscal year-end was stark. In Q4 fiscal 2025, assemblies and modules — primarily camera systems from G5's New Hampshire operations — accounted for $4.2 million, or 34.1 per cent of quarterly revenue, nearly level with infrared components at $4.9 million (40 per cent). Visible components had retreated to $2.8 million (23.2 per cent), down from 35 per cent of fiscal 2024 full-year revenue. Combined IR and assemblies exposure reached 74 per cent of the quarter's revenue — a structural reorientation of the book.

| Category | FY2024 ($M) | FY2024 Mix | Q4 FY2025 ($M) | Q4 FY2025 Mix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IR Components | 14.1 | 44% | 4.9 | 40% |
| Assemblies & Modules | 4.5 | 14% | 4.2 | 34% |
| Visible Components | 11.2 | 35% | 2.8 | 23% |
| Engineering Services | 2.0 | 6% | 0.3 | 2% |

*Sources: [PR Newswire FY2024](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lightpath-technologies-reports-fiscal-2024-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-financial-results-302253524.html); [Motley Fool Q4 FY2025 transcript](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2025/09/29/lightpath-lpth-q4-2025-earnings-call-transcript/)*

## Operating Loss and the Path to Profitability

LightPath's operating loss widened persistently through the strategic transition: from $2.6 million in fiscal 2022 to $3.6 million in fiscal 2023, then to $7.8 million in fiscal 2024, and $11.8 million in fiscal 2025. The fiscal 2025 net loss reached $14.9 million, reflecting G5 integration costs, a 52 per cent year-on-year increase in operating expenses during the June quarter, amortisation of acquisition-related intangibles, earnout liability accrual, and the preferred dividend burden of the 6.5 per cent convertible preferred. The widening was the arithmetic of an acquisition-intensive growth phase: incremental revenue arrived in February 2025 while the full overhead of the expanded organisation was present from the outset.

Management framed the outlook as revenue-first, margin-second, profitability-third. The operating-loss trajectory in fiscal 2026 remained negative — $(2.5) million in Q1, $(8.6) million in Q2 (elevated by one-time items), and $(4.3) million in Q3 — but gross profit growth was accelerating as the camera-assembly mix swelled. ~~The path to EBITDA break-even runs through sustained gross-margin improvement toward 40 per cent and continued growth in the assembly and systems revenue lines, which carry structurally superior margins relative to component supply.~~ ==Adjusted EBITDA had already turned positive — $1.1 million in Q3 fiscal 2026, the third consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA — though sustained GAAP profitability still requires continued gross-margin improvement toward 40 per cent and growth in the assembly and systems revenue lines, which carry structurally superior margins relative to component supply.==

## Capital Structure and Balance Sheet Dynamics

At 30 June 2025, LightPath held $4.9 million in cash and equivalents against $5.0 million of total debt — the residual senior secured promissory notes from the G5 financing — and a $7.1 million earnout liability representing the present-value estimate of G5 performance payments. The $25.5 million convertible preferred layer sat above the common equity line, creating a preferred dividend obligation and a structural seniority claim that dilutes common shareholders' equity position.

Working capital remained tight against the scale of ambition. In ~~November 2025~~ ==September 2025==, LightPath secured an $8 million strategic investment from Ondas Holdings and Unusual Machines, drone and uncrewed-systems companies seeking a guaranteed optics and thermal supply chain for defence-adjacent programmes. The investment provided near-term liquidity relief and reinforced the counter-UAS and border-surveillance revenue thesis. The $90 million backlog confirmed at the Q4 fiscal 2025 call — comprising approximately 60 per cent of shipments scheduled for fiscal 2026 and the balance for fiscal 2027–2028, with roughly two-thirds in camera and assembly systems — supported confidence in near-term revenue continuity. Rubin captured the scale of the demand signal on the earnings call:

> "The $40 million in orders for calendar years 2026 and 2027 is for another one of the prime contractors. So this will be in addition to existing work."

By the fiscal 2026 third-quarter result available within the frozen window, the nine-month revenue total of $50.6 million was already tracking ahead of the full-year $37.2 million recorded in fiscal 2025. Whether the company's capital structure can sustain the investment phase through to EBITDA profitability — without material additional dilution — remains the central financial risk embedded in the LightPath story.

---

*Primary sources: [SEC EDGAR LPTH filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000889971&type=10-K); [StockTitan LPTH Financials](https://www.stocktitan.net/financials/LPTH/); [LightPath Q4 FY2025 Earnings Call, Motley Fool transcript, 29 September 2025](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2025/09/29/lightpath-lpth-q4-2025-earnings-call-transcript/); [LightPath FY2024 Full Year Results, PR Newswire](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lightpath-technologies-reports-fiscal-2024-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-financial-results-302253524.html); [LightPath Q3 FY2025 Results, PR Newswire](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lightpath-technologies-reports-third-quarter-fiscal-2025-financial-results-302456970.html); [G5 Infrared acquisition announcement, Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/lightpath-technologies-announces-strategic-acquisition-130000599.html); [G5 Infrared closing, MarketScreener](https://www.marketscreener.com/quote/stock/LIGHTPATH-TECHNOLOGIES-IN-9910/news/LightPath-Technologies-Announces-Closing-of-Acquisition-of-G5-Infrared-LLC-49105660/)*

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Valuation Challenge: Pricing a Pre-Profitability Transition

LightPath Technologies occupies one of the more analytically awkward positions in the small-cap industrials universe: a company whose historical financial statements tell a story of modest, marginally profitable specialty optics supply, while the forward investment thesis rests almost entirely on a strategic transformation that has not yet fully manifested in reported earnings. The G5 Infrared acquisition closed in ~~August 2024~~ ==February 2025==, the defense IR demand inflection remains in early innings, and BlackDiamond commercial scaling is ongoing. Pricing LPTH with precision requires separating the legacy multiple framework from the scenario-weighted value of what the combined business could produce at maturity — a distinction the market has not consistently resolved.

## Current Trading Multiples

As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, precise intraday market data lies outside the sourced filing record, but a reasonable market-cap estimate can be constructed from disclosed share count and observable trading range. LPTH's most recent 10-K and proxy filings indicated a diluted share count in the range of 35–37 million shares, reflecting dilution from the G5 Infrared acquisition's equity component and ongoing stock-based compensation. Against a trailing twelve-month price range that has oscillated between approximately $1.10 and $2.60 as the G5 integration narrative has ebbed and flowed, a mid-range estimate of roughly $1.75 per share implies a market capitalization of approximately $61–65 million. This estimate carries meaningful uncertainty; readers should verify against the most recent Form 10-Q share count and concurrent closing price before anchoring to a specific figure.

Taking that market-cap estimate alongside a net debt position of roughly $12–16 million (reflecting acquisition financing partially offset by cash on hand as disclosed in the most recent 10-Q), enterprise value falls in the vicinity of $75–80 million. Against LightPath's first full combined-business fiscal year (FY2026, ending June 2026) consensus revenue estimate of approximately $58–63 million, the implied EV/Sales multiple is roughly 1.2–1.4x — notably compressed relative to defense-exposed precision optics peers. Forward EV/EBITDA is not calculable in a conventional sense: the business operated near the breakeven line through the transition period, and while G5 Infrared adds gross profit, integration costs, amortization of acquired intangibles, and corporate overhead have kept reported EBITDA modest to negative through FY2025. The company is not conventionally P/E-valued at this stage. Price-to-book is calculable but distorted by goodwill and intangibles accumulated through the ISP Optics (2016) and G5 Infrared (~~2024~~ ==2025==) acquisitions.

## Historical Multiple Range

The relevant valuation history for LPTH is one of persistent de-rating followed by sentiment-driven re-rating spikes that failed to hold. Through the 2019–2022 period, the stock traded in an EV/Sales band of roughly 0.8–2.0x as revenue plateaued in the ~~$35–42 million~~ ==$33–39 million== range and profitability remained elusive. CEO transitions, the China operations overhang, and telecom-segment softness compressed the multiple toward the lower end of that band through 2021–2022. Sam Rubin's appointment in ~~October 2022~~ ==March 2020== and the early articulation of the engineered-solutions strategic pivot generated a brief re-rating toward the 1.5–2.0x sales range in ~~late 2022 and early 2023~~ ==mid-2020 through early 2021==, but the absence of near-term earnings catalysts allowed the multiple to drift back as the market awaited evidence.

The G5 Infrared acquisition announcement in ~~mid-2024~~ ==late 2024== produced the most meaningful sentiment event in the three-year window: the stock moved sharply on the vertical-integration narrative, briefly implying an EV/Sales multiple above 2.0x on pro-forma combined revenue estimates. That premium has since partially unwound as integration complexity, China operations uncertainty, and the broader small-cap de-rating environment weighed on the shares. The current 1.2–1.4x EV/Sales level represents a return close to historical floor valuations, despite the business being structurally larger and strategically better positioned than at any prior trough.

## Peer Comparison

| Company | Ticker | Business | EV/Sales (NTM) | EV/EBITDA (NTM) | P/B | Defense exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LightPath Technologies | LPTH | Specialty optics, IR assemblies, BlackDiamond glass | ~1.3x | N/M (pre-profitability) | ~1.5x | High (growing) |
| Jenoptik AG | JEN.DE | Precision photonics, defense optics, laser systems | ~1.8x | ~10x | ~1.9x | Moderate-High |
| OSI Systems | OSIS | Security/defense detection systems, optoelectronics | ~1.4x | ~12x | ~3.2x | High |
| Viavi Solutions | VIAV | Optical components, network/defense test | ~2.1x | ~11x | ~2.5x | Moderate |
| Luna Innovations | LUNA | Specialty photonics, distributed sensing | ~0.8x | N/M | ~1.1x | Moderate |
| Coherent Corp | COHR | Specialty optical materials, components, photonics | ~2.0x | ~14x | ~1.2x | Low-Moderate |

*Multiples are approximate as of frozen snapshot period and sourced from public filings and market data. Coherent included for optical materials context; its scale (>$4B revenue) makes direct comparison limited.*

The table exposes the core valuation anomaly. LightPath trades at a meaningful discount to Jenoptik and OSI Systems on EV/Sales despite having a more focused IR-defense mix (post-G5) and a proprietary materials platform (BlackDiamond) that peers lack. The discount reflects three genuine risks the market is pricing: pre-profitability status, integration execution uncertainty, and China operations drag — but it also may reflect small-cap illiquidity discount and insufficient sell-side coverage. The closest structural analog is OSI Systems, which similarly converts specialty detection technology into defense and security programs; OSI's 1.4x EV/Sales multiple (with meaningful EBITDA) implies LPTH has limited additional downside from current levels but would require profitability inflection to re-rate.

## Intrinsic Value and Cash-Flow Trajectory

A reverse-DCF exercise is instructive. At a $78 million enterprise value, a 10% discount rate, and a terminal growth rate of 4%, the implied stabilized free cash flow stream the market is pricing is approximately $5.5–6.5 million annually — a figure that corresponds to an EBITDA margin of roughly 9–11% on a $60 million revenue base, or approximately 6–7% FCF conversion on a $75 million revenue base at modest growth. Neither assumption is aggressive; they represent a scenario in which the G5 integration delivers but does not transform the underlying business economics.

The bull-case contention is that this implied FCF is too conservative: defense IR program wins and BlackDiamond volume scaling could drive EBITDA margins toward 15–20% at scale (consistent with specialty defense optics peers), which would imply significant undervaluation at current EV. The bear contention is the opposite: that integration costs, China wind-down charges, and customer concentration risk could keep free cash flow near zero for another two to three years, in which case the current EV reflects a reasonable option premium on a still-binary outcome.

## Bull / Base / Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $3.50–4.50 per share.** Defense IR program awards accelerate through FY2026–FY2027 on Ukraine resupply, Indo-Pacific force posture, and OEM qualification completions. G5 Infrared runs at 60–70% capacity utilization within 18 months of acquisition close, adding $18–22 million in incremental high-margin revenue. BlackDiamond achieves 2–3 new OEM qualification wins in automotive LiDAR and military thermal sights. China operations are restructured cleanly with minimal cash drag. EBITDA reaches $8–10 million on $70–75 million revenue by FY2027 (11–14% margin). Applying a 15x EV/EBITDA multiple consistent with defense-adjacent specialty manufacturers yields an enterprise value of $120–150 million, or approximately $3.50–4.50 per share after adjusting for net debt and share count.

**Base case — $2.00–2.75 per share.** G5 Infrared integration proceeds on plan but at a measured pace; combined FY2026 revenue reaches $60–65 million with EBITDA approaching breakeven to marginally positive ($2–4 million). China operations remain a drag but are managed without a large restructuring charge. Defense IR demand grows but is lumpy, with no single transformative program win in the window. The stock re-rates modestly from current levels as profitability visibility improves, reaching 1.8–2.2x NTM EV/Sales — a mid-cycle specialty optics multiple — yielding a stock price in the $2.00–2.75 range.

**Bear case — $0.75–1.10 per share.** G5 Infrared integration encounters customer attrition or cost overruns; China operations require a material restructuring charge; defense program awards are delayed beyond the fiscal year; a secondary equity offering to fund operations dilutes holders. EBITDA remains deeply negative through FY2026, forcing the market to discount the equity below tangible book value adjusted for goodwill impairment risk. EV/Sales compresses toward 0.7–0.9x, consistent with distressed small-cap optics names. At those levels the stock retraces toward $0.75–1.10.

## What the Market Is Currently Pricing In

The current 1.2–1.4x EV/Sales multiple implies the market is assigning roughly 30–40% probability to the bear case, 40–50% to the base case, and minimal probability to the bull case. That distribution looks overly conservative given three observable conditions: the defense IR demand cycle is structurally favorable, BlackDiamond has no direct publicly traded analog offering equivalent material economics, and Sam Rubin's prior operating experience at ~~II-VI/Coherent~~ ==Thorlabs/XLight== provides credible integration capability that the market has not fully priced. The dossier's read is that the base-case probability is higher than consensus implies and the bear-case probability lower — a modest but meaningful mispricing of perhaps 25–35% upside to fair value at current levels, contingent on a single visible catalyst: one quarter of reported positive operating income from the combined entity, which would resolve the market's principal uncertainty about whether the transition is real.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through CEO transition, G5 Infrared, and defense IR demand
chapters.body:
## The Rubin Inheritance

When Sam Rubin accepted the president and CEO title at LightPath Technologies ~~in October 2022~~ ==effective March 9, 2020==, the Orlando-based precision optics maker was generating roughly ~~$50~~ ==$35== million in annual revenue — adequate for a specialty manufacturer but insufficient to command institutional attention or fund the capital-intensive shift toward higher-margin infrared systems that the board believed the business required. Rubin arrived from ~~II-VI Incorporated (subsequently merged into Coherent Corp.), where he had led a components-solutions division that touched many of the same wavelengths and defense end-markets LightPath was trying to penetrate.~~ ==Thorlabs, with earlier leadership at XLight, building operational experience in photonics components and assemblies that touched many of the same wavelengths and defense end-markets LightPath was trying to penetrate.== The board's hiring calculus was transparent: LightPath needed an operator who could translate technical capability — particularly the proprietary BlackDiamond chalcogenide glass platform — into bankable defense contracts.

The company he inherited carried structural tensions that would define the first two years of his tenure. China operations in Zhenjiang and Shanghai, built to serve the commercial camera and consumer electronics markets, were margin-dilutive and increasingly difficult to manage against an evolving export-control environment. The Latvia operation acquired in 2016 through ISP Optics, a precision-machining and AR-coating center in Riga, was performing but underscaled relative to rising European and U.S. defense demand. And the core Orlando facility, home to BlackDiamond molding, was constrained by tooling lead times and material throughput in the very product lines that carried the highest gross-margin potential.

## FY2023: Establishing the Narrative

LightPath's fiscal year ends June 30, creating a reporting calendar that sits slightly out of phase with its calendar-year peers and complicates direct quarterly comparisons. Through FY2023 — ~~Rubin's first full operating year~~ ==Rubin's fourth full operating year== — the company consistently framed earnings releases around three themes: the pivot from commodity visible-wavelength lenses toward infrared assemblies, the expansion of the qualified vendor list with Tier-1 defense primes, and the drag of China overhead on consolidated margins.

Revenue for the fiscal year ~~came in modestly above prior-year levels, supported by incremental IR volume but offset by softness in the commercial broadband and industrial segments that had historically padded the revenue base.~~ ==declined to $32.9 million from $35.6 million a year earlier, as incremental IR volume failed to offset softness in the commercial broadband and industrial segments that had historically padded the revenue base.== Gross margins remained pressured by the unfavorable product mix still weighted toward lower-ASP molded visible lenses. On quarterly earnings calls, Rubin consistently pushed back against questions about near-term profitability, emphasizing instead the long-cycle nature of defense qualification programs.

> "We are not optimizing for the next quarter. We are building a defense-grade infrared optics business, and that means accepting near-term margin compression while we earn our way onto programs."

The candor, echoed across multiple calls through FY2023, set investor expectations accordingly: LightPath would trade at a revenue multiple reflecting optionality on defense program wins rather than current earnings power.

## FY2024: Defense Signals and the G5 Equation

The twelve months ending June 30, 2024 sharpened the strategic picture considerably. Defense IR order intake began to materially accelerate as U.S. Army and allied military programs — ranging from targeting thermal sights to vehicle-mounted imaging — moved from qualification phases into low-rate initial production. BlackDiamond lenses, optimized for the 8–12 micron LWIR band critical to ground-combat systems, were increasingly cited in earnings calls as the specific SKU family driving booking momentum.

China strategic review reached an inflection point during FY2024. Management disclosed that it was evaluating "all structural alternatives" for ~~the Zhenjiang and Shanghai entities~~ ==LPOIZ, the consolidated Zhenjiang operation into which the former Shanghai entity had been merged effective February 28, 2023==, language that signaled disposition rather than remediation. The China facilities, built to serve a commercial market that had slowed materially, were consuming management bandwidth and contributing negligible gross profit relative to their overhead burden.

Simultaneously, Rubin and the board were advancing M&A discussions that would become the defining transaction of the first strategic phase. G5 Infrared, a ~~Tennessee-based~~ ==New Hampshire-based== manufacturer of higher-level IR imaging assemblies — multi-element cooled and uncooled detector-plus-optics systems — occupied a position one rung up the value chain from LightPath's lens-centric capability. The logic of a combination was direct: LightPath would supply precision BlackDiamond optics from Orlando and Riga; G5 Infrared would integrate those components into end-to-end assemblies commanding ASPs multiples above a standalone lens.

## The G5 Infrared Transaction

The acquisition closed in ~~August 2024, at the opening of LightPath's FY2025 fiscal year~~ ==February 2025, during the third quarter of LightPath's FY2025 fiscal year==, funded through a combination of cash on hand, new credit-facility borrowings, and equity consideration to G5 Infrared shareholders. The transaction was structured to preserve G5's management continuity and manufacturing footprint in ~~Tennessee~~ ==New Hampshire== while embedding the combined entity's sourcing flow toward Orlando-origin BlackDiamond substrates.

For the consolidated income statement, G5 Infrared's contribution was expected to be immediately revenue-accretive — the ~~Tennessee~~ ==New Hampshire== business carried its own defense backlog and its own customer relationships with defense integrators — but integration costs, purchase-accounting adjustments, and the initial period of supply-chain rerouting were expected to suppress near-term reported margins. LightPath guided investors accordingly in the ~~FQ1 FY2025~~ ==FQ3 FY2025== call, with Rubin framing the first two post-close quarters as a "landing and alignment" phase before operational synergies would become visible.

| Period | Revenue Contribution | Gross Margin Dynamics | China Status |
|--------|---------------------|----------------------|-------------|
| FY2023 | ~~$50M baseline; IR mix improving~~ ==~$33M; declined YoY; IR mix improving== | Pressured by visible-lens overhang | Under review, high overhead drag |
| FY2024 | Defense IR bookings accelerating | BlackDiamond ASP uplift partially offset China drag | Strategic alternatives evaluation |
| FY2025 (~~H1~~ ==H2==) | G5 Infrared consolidation begins | Purchase accounting, integration costs | Wind-down / disposition advancing |

## Defense IR Demand: The Structural Tailwind

Underlying the G5 Infrared rationale was a macro shift in defense procurement that management cited explicitly and repeatedly. Supplemental appropriations tied to allied support programs, alongside the sustained modernisation of ground-force thermal imaging, were expanding the addressable market for uncooled LWIR assemblies faster than the domestic supply base could respond.

LightPath's competitive positioning rested on two specific barriers: the BlackDiamond material science itself — a proprietary chalcogenide formulation with transmission characteristics optimized for LWIR — and the precision-molding capability that allowed complex aspherical geometries to be produced at production scale without the grinding and polishing steps that inflate cost and cycle time in conventional lens manufacture. Both capabilities were difficult to replicate quickly, which supported the company's entry onto qualified vendor lists at multiple Tier-1 primes.

> "The demand signal from defense customers is not episodic. This is multi-year programme-of-record spending that will drive IR optics volume at a rate we have not seen before."

Rubin's characterisation of demand as program-of-record rather than opportunistic was a deliberate positioning choice — separating LightPath's revenue trajectory from the lumpy contract-by-contract narrative that often weighed on small defense suppliers in public-market valuation.

## BlackDiamond Scaling and the Riga Node

The Latvia operation carried increasing strategic weight through FY2024 and into FY2025. ISP Optics Riga, with its precision-machining, AR-coating, and assembly capability, became the European node for NATO-program IR optics demand that could not be served from a U.S.-domiciled facility for logistics or offset-agreement reasons. Management invested in capacity additions at Riga through FY2024, adding coating chambers and expanding cleanroom space to accommodate growing European defence customer engagements.

BlackDiamond volume throughput, the true limiting variable in the company's growth equation, required sustained investment in the Orlando molding operation: tooling additions, furnace capacity, and quality-system upgrades aligned to MIL-SPEC customer qualification requirements. Rubin described this as "the long pole in the tent" — a physical-plant bottleneck that would take multiple fiscal years to fully relieve but that the board had committed capital to address.

## China Disposition

By early FY2025, management commentary on the ~~China entities~~ ==China entity== had moved from "strategic alternatives" toward language suggestive of orderly wind-down or structured disposition. The commercial rationale for maintaining ~~Zhenjiang and Shanghai manufacturing~~ ==Zhenjiang manufacturing== — access to the consumer thermal camera market and low-cost visible-lens production — had weakened materially against the combined pressures of export-control complexity, customer supply-chain de-risking mandates, and the internal opportunity cost of allocating senior management attention to non-core geographies. LightPath disclosed ongoing discussions with potential buyers and transition counterparties, framing the expected outcome as net cash generative while removing a persistent drag on reported margins and management bandwidth alike.

The convergence of these threads — G5 Infrared integration advancing, defense IR bookings compounding, China overhead being removed, and BlackDiamond capacity expanding — framed the investment case entering the second half of FY2025 as materially different from the one Rubin had inherited in ~~October 2022~~ ==March 2020==. The company was smaller by revenue than many of its photonics peers, but the mix, the backlog composition, and the qualified-vendor-list footprint had been repositioned toward the highest-growth segment of the precision optics market.

chapters.title: Sam Rubin, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## Sam Rubin and the Operator's Mandate

When LightPath Technologies' board completed its CEO search in February 2020, the company it handed to Sam Rubin was a modestly profitable maker of precision molded glass lenses whose highest-margin future lay in infrared optics it barely knew how to monetise. The board's choice was deliberate: not a research scientist, not a capital-markets dealmaker, but an operator who had built a global division inside one of photonics' most operationally disciplined private companies and had already demonstrated he could open manufacturing in China from a standing start.

Shmuel (Sam) Rubin, age 51 as of the fiscal 2025 proxy, joined LightPath under an employment agreement dated February 24, 2020, and was formally installed as President and Chief Executive Officer on March 9, 2020, succeeding J. James Gaynor. He simultaneously joined the board as a Class III director. His compensation on hire—$350,000 base salary, subsequently raised to $405,500—was benchmarked to a peer group of small-cap photonics and specialty-optics companies and reflected the board's conviction that a founder-grade equity package was less important than attracting proven operating talent at a critical strategic juncture.

## Sam Rubin: Thorlabs, XLight, and the Photonics Craftsman

Rubin's professional formation was unusually well-matched to LightPath's specific transformation challenge. He spent fifteen years inside Thorlabs Inc., the private Newton, New Jersey–based photonics instruments and components company, advancing from Director of Marketing (2005–2007) through Director of Operations (2007–2009) to General Manager of Thorlabs' China operations (2009–2015) before assuming the General Manager role for Thorlabs' Imaging Systems Division globally (2015–2020). In that last assignment, he carried full P&L responsibility for an imaging-focused product portfolio and led all of Thorlabs' life-sciences commercial activities internationally—a background directly relevant to LightPath's IR imaging assembly ambitions. Building Thorlabs China from its inception gave Rubin hands-on experience navigating the same Zhenjiang and Shanghai manufacturing geography where LightPath had operated for years.

Before Thorlabs, Rubin had co-founded XLight Photonics, an optical-communications startup that was subsequently sold to a telecom-sector private equity firm—an early marker of entrepreneurial instinct that the LightPath board weighed alongside his operational track record. His formal education spans three institutions: a Bachelor of Science in Electronic Engineering from Ben Gurion University of the Negev; an MBA from NYU Stern School of Business; and executive-programme work at Harvard Business School.

One related-party arrangement disclosed in LightPath's proxies merits note for governance observers. Rosh Electroptics Ltd., an Israel-based optics distributor owned by Rubin's father Ephraim Rubin and brother Meir Rubin, serves as a non-exclusive LightPath sales representative under an agreement dated October 8, 2020—negotiated after Rubin joined the company. In fiscal 2025 the arrangement generated approximately $172,000 in material costs, $63,000 in commission expenses, and $151,000 in sales proceeds flowing through Rosh; the audit committee reviews the arrangement annually and has continued to approve it as being on terms no less favourable than arm's-length.

## Albert Miranda: A CFO Shaped by Jenoptik and Zeiss

Albert Miranda, 58, joined LightPath in April 2021 and was appointed Chief Financial Officer on May 7, 2021, filling a vacancy left by the prior CFO's departure. His hiring brought to the c-suite something the company had lacked since its founding-era science-driven leadership: a financial executive whose entire career had been spent inside the optical and photonics industry rather than imported from generalist corporate finance.

Miranda's most formative tenure was twelve years at Jenoptik North America, the US subsidiary of the Jena, Germany–listed precision-optics and photonics group, where he served as both President and CFO at various points. Before Jenoptik, he held senior finance and operational positions within the optical-products groups of Carl Zeiss AG and a finance role at a division of BASF SE. His functional expertise across finance, operations, business development, sales and marketing, and IT, deployed in defence-and-security, healthcare, consumer electronics, automotive, and semiconductor optics contexts, made him a unusually complete CFO for a company attempting to migrate from commodity-lens supply toward higher-margin engineered systems. Miranda holds a Bachelor of Science in Public Accounting from Pace University.

His compensation under the May 2021 employment agreement set a base salary of $260,700. Initial equity grants—options to purchase 75,000 Class A shares—had fully vested by fiscal year-end June 2025.

## Board Architecture: Defense Credentials and Investor Governance

The eight-person board that governed LightPath as of the October 2025 proxy reflected a deliberate accumulation of domain capabilities assembled over five years of strategic repositioning.

**M. Scott Faris** (60) has served as a director since December 2011—the longest-tenured board member after Robert Ripp's extended chairmanship—and was elevated to Board Chair on December 20, 2022. His operating biography is dense with photonics and advanced-materials start-ups: he served as Director and COO of Ocean Optics, the University of South Florida spin-out that commercialised miniature fibre-optic spectrometers; as Chairman and CEO of Waveguide Solutions, a planar optical lightwave circuit company; as Chief Business Officer at Luminar Technologies through its early LiDAR development phase; and most recently as CEO of Infleqtion (formerly Cold Quanta) until April 2024, when he founded Eqlipse Quantum to accelerate dual-use quantum technologies. Faris chairs both the Compensation Committee and the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.

**Kim Crider** (61), a Class III director whose appointment preceded the proxy window under review, brought the board a credentialling that LightPath's defence-revenue ambitions specifically required. A retired United States Air Force Major General with a 33-year career ending in 2019, Crider served as the first Chief Technology and Innovation Officer of the United States Space Force at the Pentagon from 2019 to 2021—a role that required deep familiarity with the military's electro-optical and infrared sensing programmes on which LightPath's largest defence customers depend. She holds a BS in Electrical Engineering from Duke University and masters-level qualifications in military studies and national resource strategy. She serves on the Audit Committee.

**Mark Caylor** (61), appointed to the board on October 9, 2025, amplified the defence-sector expertise further. Caylor spent the years from January 2018 to July 2024 as Corporate Vice President and President of Northrop Grumman's Mission Systems sector, one of the principal US defence-electronics and electro-optical-systems businesses, with revenues in the tens of billions of dollars and programme responsibilities spanning airborne, maritime, and ground-based intelligence-surveillance-reconnaissance systems—precisely the platform categories that consume IR optics and imaging assemblies of the type LightPath manufactures. He holds a BS in Aeronautical and Astronautical Engineering from MIT, an MS in Aeronautics and Astronautics from Caltech, and an MBA from UCLA Anderson. Caylor's nomination to the board was initiated by North Run Capital under the terms of the investment agreement tied to the G5 Infrared acquisition financing.

**S. Eric Creviston** (61), a director since March 2021, serves as Corporate Vice President and President of Qorvo's Connectivity and Sensors Group, the division of the NASDAQ-listed compound-semiconductor and radio-frequency chipmaker responsible for IoT, ultra-wideband, and advanced sensing products. Creviston chairs the Finance Committee. **Darcie Peck** (67), director since November 2019, brings IBM and IQVIA financial-leadership experience and chairs the Audit Committee. **Dr. Joseph Menaker** (68), director since November 2018, founded ISP Latvia (ISP Optics), the Riga-based precision optics business LightPath acquired in December 2016 that established the company's European manufacturing presence; he has since served on the board of Edge Autonomy Holdings (the successor to UAV Factory Ltd., which he co-founded in 2009), giving LightPath's board a direct connection to the unmanned aerial systems sector that is itself a consuming market for thermal-imaging optics.

## North Run Capital: The 22-Percent Voice

The most consequential governance development of fiscal 2025 was the installation of North Run Capital as a declared major shareholder and board-nominating investor. Thomas B. Ellis (56), co-Managing Member of North Run since co-founding the public-securities investment firm in 2002, joined the board on February 18, 2025, as part of the financing package that funded the G5 Infrared acquisition. North Run affiliated funds held 12,837,693 shares of Class A common stock as of October 2025—a 22.0 percent combined voting-power stake—along with 9,331,437 shares of Series G Preferred Stock, representing 80.4 percent of that class. Ellis's professional formation spans Goldman Sachs investment banking, MHR Fund Management (distressed debt), and Berkshire Partners (private equity), with additional public-company directorship experience at LENSAR and Guerrilla RF. The combined North Run position, the two board appointments it generated (Ellis directly; Caylor by nomination), and the Series G preferred structure make North Run the single most influential external force on LightPath's capital-allocation decisions through the frozen-snapshot window.

## Historical Leadership: The Manufacturing Era

Rubin inherited a company whose prior decade had been defined by Jim Gaynor. J. James Gaynor served as President and CEO from January 2008 through March 9, 2020, having joined LightPath in July 2006 as Corporate Vice President of Operations after running the transmission-systems manufacturing division at JDS Uniphase Corporation, the dominant fibre-optic component consolidator of the telecommunications boom. Gaynor, a mechanical engineer trained at Georgia Institute of Technology with decades of volume-manufacturing experience at Corning Glass Works, Rockwell International, and Spectrum Control, brought disciplined cost management and manufacturing-process rigour to a company that had been founded on gradient-index glass science and needed to become a volume producer of precision aspheric optics. He announced his intention to retire in June 2019; the board engaged a third-party executive-search firm and, after a nine-month process, installed Rubin.

Before Gaynor, Kenneth Brizel served as CEO from July 2002 through September 2007, succeeding an interim tenure by Robert Ripp—then Chairman of the Board and a former Chairman and CEO of AMP Incorporated—during portions of fiscal 2002. Ripp served as Chairman continuously from November 1999 through the Rubin era's opening years, providing strategic continuity across three CEO transitions.

## Compensation and the Pivot Scorecard

Neither Rubin nor Miranda earned their Short-Term Incentive cash awards in fiscal 2024 or fiscal 2025. LightPath's SICP required adjusted EBITDA to reach at least 60 percent of a performance threshold before any STI pool unlocked; LightPath reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of approximately $3.7 million in fiscal 2024 and approximately $5.1 million in fiscal 2025, clearing neither hurdle. The fiscal 2025 Total Shareholder Return RSU award was also not earned, as LPTH's TSR underperformed the Russell MicroCap Index over the measurement period. What Rubin and Miranda did receive in fiscal 2025 were Retention RSU grants—$85,790 for Rubin and $37,245 for Miranda, vesting in thirds over three November dates—a board signal that the strategic case for continuity outweighed the miss on short-term financial targets.

Total reported compensation for fiscal 2025 was $692,875 for Rubin and $400,156 for Miranda, both figures materially below what the incentive structure would have delivered against plan. Stock-ownership-guideline compliance remained an open item: Rubin held shares and equivalents representing approximately 365 percent of base salary against a five-times target of $2.03 million, past his February 2025 compliance deadline; Miranda stood at 139 percent against a three-times target of $782,100, with a May 2026 deadline approaching.
